title: Woods Hole research ship heads to Lake Superior to hunt neutrinos
excerpt: The R/V Neil Armstrong is making its first Great Lakes voyage, carrying Cape Cod science into fresh water for an experiment probing the universe.
content:
Nov. 5, 2026, 6:02 a.m. ET

  • The Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution research vessel R/V Neil Armstrong has traveled from the Atlantic Ocean to Lake Superior.
  • This is the vessel's first time operating in a completely freshwater environment, requiring adaptations for buoyancy and filtration.
  • The ship will assist scientists in deploying large underwater detector arrays to search for elusive subatomic particles called neutrinos.
  • Researchers believe studying neutrinos in Lake Superior could help answer fundamental questions about the universe.

Nobody would look at a map of Lake Superior and expect to find a Woods Hole research vessel there.

Yet that's exactly where R/V Neil Armstrong has headed. After departing Cape Cod on Oct. 28, the 238-foot Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution vessel began an 11-day, 2,531-nautical-mile journey far inland to Duluth, Minnesota, following a route through rivers, canals and locks. It had just passed Quebec City on Nov. 2 and was moving on to Montreal.

By the time it reaches its destination around Nov. 9, the Neil Armstrong will be floating more than 1,000 miles from the Atlantic Ocean. For a vessel that normally operates in salt water, it's an assignment that feels a bit like stepping into an alien habitat, with a purpose tied less to the mysteries of the sea than to the mysteries of the cosmos.

"This is certainly one of the most unusual journeys in the R/V Neil Armstrong’s history. The vessel was designed for open-ocean research. This is its first time making the journey to the Great Lakes, or operating in a totally freshwater environment," said Rob Munier, WHOI Vice President of Marine Operations and Facilities, who wrote by email from aboard the vessel.

In its 11 years of service, Munier said, "the ship has traveled from the high-latitude waters around Greenland, including Baffin Bay and the Irminger Sea, to warmer regions of the Atlantic, Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico, engaging in every oceanographic discipline, deploying and recovering complex observing systems, and testing new technologies."

"The ship has demonstrated its ability to support research in some of the ocean's most challenging environments, but this voyage puts that versatility to work in an entirely new setting," Munier said.

R/V Neil Armstrong helps in search for neutrinos

From the Atlantic Ocean, the route takes the vessel through the Gulf of St. Lawrence and up the St. Lawrence River, then through Lake Ontario, the Welland Canal, Lake Erie, the Detroit River, Lake St. Clair, the St. Clair River, Lake Huron, the St. Marys River and the Soo Locks before reaching Lake Superior.

Once it arrives, the crew will help scientists search for neutrinos, elusive subatomic particles that rarely interact with matter and remain among the most difficult building blocks of the universe to detect.

The project, known as the Experimental Neutrino Detector, is led by the University of Minnesota Duluth and sponsored by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, in cooperation with the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science, Fermilab and Brookhaven National Laboratory.

For WHOI, the assignment represents an unlikely convergence of disciplines, applying ocean-forged engineering and operational capabilities on a freshwater lake, in support of a physics experiment focused on questions that extend far beyond Earth's oceans.

The Neil Armstrong’s deck and engineering officers, Munier said, have developed a detailed voyage plan as they navigate new territory, including required communications with authorities, lock protocols, speed restrictions, and environmental considerations. The ship has two WHOI captains aboard and will also take on local pilots for portions of the transit to help navigate the unfamiliar waterways. 

R/V Neil Armstrong adapts to Lake Superior's fresh water

"One of the biggest challenges is adapting a vessel designed for saltwater ocean operations to the very different conditions of the Great Lakes. Freshwater is less dense than seawater, providing less buoyancy, and the lakes can produce steep, short-period waves that behave differently from open-ocean swells," Munier explained.

The ship's water filtration systems also had to be modified for the freshwater environment, he said, and crew and shoreside teams are implementing procedures designed to prevent major issues along the way.

"Because the captain and crew have so much experience operating in a wide variety of environments, we are confident we will be able to adapt to the expected and unexpected challenges of transiting to and working in the Great Lakes," he said.

Why scientists are studying neutrinos in Lake Superior

The scientists the vessel is supporting aren't studying neutrinos simply because they are difficult to find. Researchers believe the particles may help answer some of the biggest questions in physics, including why the universe is composed mostly of matter rather than antimatter, and what happened in the moments after the Big Bang.

Detecting them is no easy task. Because neutrinos can pass through objects — even entire planets — with barely any interaction, scientists need enormous natural environments to improve their odds of spotting them. In this experiment, Lake Superior's vast volume of water will become part of the detection system.

Before the Neil Armstrong left Woods Hole, engineers in WHOI's Mooring Operations and Engineering Group took on the task of creating five detector arrays that will be installed on the floor of Lake Superior. Each frame rises about 30 feet tall and weighs about 8,000 pounds when equipped with instruments.

Neutrino detector arrays shipped by truck from Woods Hole

WHOI Senior Engineer Don Peters, the lead engineer of the project, said by email from the vessel that the frame design is modular, allowing it to be shipped by truck. 

"It is made up of nine, 3-meter-high main modules assembled into tiers of three modules and then stacked, and three 1-meter-high 'halo' modules that form the top tier. Six steel-foot plates spread the load on the sediment of the lake floor," he said.

Each main module is in the shape of a hexagon.

Each hexagon has beach ball-sized spheres called digital optical modules at its six corners. In total, each detector array has 18 digital optical modules.

John Kemp, group operations leader for WHOI's Mooring and Operations Group, said by email from the vessel that the team spent months designing and fabricating the frames.

As part of the U.S. academic research fleet operated through the University-National Oceanographic Laboratory System, the R/V Neil Armstrong "is particularly well-suited for this mission because it is equipped to handle heavy equipment and features a dynamic positioning system that allows it to maintain a precise position over the deployment site," Kemp said.

Once each frame is positioned, the crew will deploy a dedicated underwater fiber-optic cable, several kilometers long, to connect each detector array to a shore station.

Munier said the voyage "demonstrates how the capabilities developed to support ocean science can enable scientific discovery in other environments."

There is also a fitting footnote. Named for Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, the vessel is now helping scientists probe not just the depths of the ocean, but the depths of the universe — about as close to the stars as an oceangoing research vessel can come.
